record_type_quote: We attempted to evaluate the replicability and generalizability of ten influential research on sensory marketing by conducting a high-powered and pre-registered replication in online settings in non-WEIRD consumers.

targets.title: Creating brand names with meaning: the use of sound symbolism
targets.evidence_quote: Klink ( 2000 ) Marketing Letters 491 citations Study 1 (H1a-m) n = 265 Undergraduate students from a Mid-Atlantic college - Hypothetical brand names including front (vs. back) vowels are associated with smallness, fastness, softness, bitterness, friendliness, and prettiness - Hypothetical brand names including back (vs. front) vowels are associated with dark color, mildness, richness, warmness, masculine, strong, and heaviness. H1a: small ( r = 0.623) H1b: dark color ( r = 0.639) H1c: mild ( r = 0.283) H1d: rich ( r = 0.819) H1e: soft ( r = 0.215) H1f: fast ( r = 0.411) H1g: warm ( r = 0.615) H1h: bitter ( r = 0.230) H1i: masculine ( r = 0.570) H1j: friendly ( r = 0.245) H1k: strong ( r = 0.230) H1l: heavy ( r = 0.796) H1m: pretty ( r = 0.336)
targets.outcome_quote: Our replication attempts successfully replicated two findings (Klink, 2000 ; Shrum et al., 2012 ) and partially replicated one of them (Yorkston and Menon, 2004 ).
targets.outcome_reasoning: The discussion explicitly classes this target as successfully replicated overall. This overall verdict takes precedence over the two reversed individual hypotheses reported in Results.
targets.target_evidence_context: Table 1: Summary of previous findings that the current research attempts to replicate.

targets.authors: Shrum, L. J., Lowrey, T. M., Luna, D., Lerman, D. B., Liu, M.
targets.title: Sound symbolism effects across languages: implications for global brand names
targets.evidence_quote: Shrum et al. ( 2012 ) International Journal of Research in Marketing 133 citations Experiment 1a n = 88 Experiment 1b n=88 Experiment 1c = 181 -Undergraduates at a French university Undergraduates at a university in the US with a substantial proportion of Hispanic students -Chinese participants who were recruited by students in a graduate research course at a university in Taipei - Front (back) vowel words are preferred for convertible/knife (4 × 4 vehicles/hammer) Choice of preferred names; F (1, 367) = 63.87, r = 0.385
targets.outcome_quote: Our replication attempts successfully replicated two findings (Klink, 2000 ; Shrum et al., 2012 ) and partially replicated one of them (Yorkston and Menon, 2004 ).
targets.outcome_reasoning: Explicit successful overall verdict; the combined target comprises three experiments in one paper.
targets.target_evidence_context: Table 1: Summary of previous findings that the current research attempts to replicate.

targets.title: Color Saturation Increases Perceived Product Size
targets.evidence_quote: Hagtvedt and Brasel ( 2017 ) Journal of Consumer Research 105 citations Study 3 n = 77 Undergraduates - High (vs. low) saturation increases product size estimates, attention, and arousal Size perception: F (1, 75) = 7.13, r = 0.295 Attention: F (1, 75) = 4.95, r = 0.249 Arousal: F (1, 75) = 7.35, r = 0.299
targets.outcome_quote: Some findings that were not successfully replicated in our research employed between-participant manipulations of sensory stimuli (Elder and Krishna, 2011 ; Hagtvedt and Brasel, 2017 ).
targets.outcome_reasoning: The authors explicitly classify this attempt as unsuccessful. Attention and arousal effects do not override the overall verdict about the central saturation-size finding.
targets.target_evidence_context: Table 1: Summary of previous findings that the current research attempts to replicate.

targets.title: Healthy-left, unhealthy-right: can displaying healthy. items to the left (vs. right) of unhealthy items nudge healthier choices?
targets.evidence_quote: Romero and Biswas ( 2016 ) Journal of Consumer Research 117 citations Study 1B n = 93 Students from a major US university - Participants tend to prefer the healthy item (broccoli salad) when it is on the left (vs. right) of the images Choice of food; x2 = 5.42, df = 1, r = 0.241
targets.outcome_quote: Two of the replicable findings adopt the within-participants manipulation of sensory stimuli (Klink, 2000 ; Shrum et al., 2012 ); though not all research on within-participants manipulation can be replicated (Romero and Biswas, 2016 ).
targets.outcome_reasoning: The discussion identifies this target as not replicated, consistent with no left-right difference in healthy choice.
targets.target_evidence_context: Table 1: Summary of previous findings that the current research attempts to replicate.

targets.title: A sound idea: phonetic effects of brand names on consumer judgments
targets.evidence_quote: Yorkston and Menon ( 2004 ) Journal of Consumer Research 528 citations Study 1 n = 126 -US University students in a lab setting -Undergraduate students in a large northeastern university - Brand names including back (vs. front) vowels are rated as higher in the attribute perception index (richness, smoothness, and creaminess) - The diagnostic information (true name, test name) and the timing of the information provided (simultaneously, afterward) modulate the effects of brand names on the attribute perception index H1: Main effect of the brand name; ( F 1, 118) = 9.39, r = 0.271 H2: Name x diagnosticity; ( F 1, 121) = 7.77, r = 0.246 H3: Name x diagnosticity x timing ( F 1, 118) = 4.78, r = 0.197
targets.outcome_quote: Our replication attempts successfully replicated two findings (Klink, 2000 ; Shrum et al., 2012 ) and partially replicated one of them (Yorkston and Menon, 2004 ).
targets.outcome_reasoning: The authors explicitly describe this target as partially replicated. The attribute-perception main effect is supported while the diagnosticity and timing interactions are absent.
targets.target_evidence_context: Table 1: Summary of previous findings that the current research attempts to replicate.

targets.title: The “visual depiction effect” in advertising: facilitating. embodied mental simulation through product orientation
targets.evidence_quote: Elder and Krishna ( 2011 ) Journal of Consumer Research 341 citations Study 4 n = 78 An online panel - Visual product depictions within advertisements, such as the manipulation of orienting a product toward a participant's dominant hand, facilitate purchase intention. Purchase intention; F (1, 76) = 14.47, r = 0.400
targets.outcome_quote: Some findings that were not successfully replicated in our research employed between-participant manipulations of sensory stimuli (Elder and Krishna, 2011 ; Hagtvedt and Brasel, 2017 ).
targets.outcome_reasoning: Explicit unsuccessful verdict; neither purchase intention nor mental simulation showed the original orientation effect.
targets.target_evidence_context: Table 1: Summary of previous findings that the current research attempts to replicate.

targets.authors: Jiang, Y., Gorn, G. J., Galli, M., Chattopadhyay, A.
targets.title: Does your company have the right logo? How and why circular- and angular-logo shapes influence brand attribute judgments
targets.evidence_quote: Jiang et al. ( 2015 ) Journal of Consumer Research 221 citations Experiment 1 n = 109 Undergraduates - Circular and angular-logo shapes influence consumers' judgment of softness-related and hardness-related product attributes Comfortableness and durability judgments: F (2, 106) = 7.63, r = 0.251
targets.outcome_quote: No studies involving visual factors, between-participant manipulation of senses, or interactions between factors could be replicated.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The set-level verdict covers this visual-logo target. The central shape-by-attribute effect failed; the incidental null effect on overall attitude is not the central finding.
targets.target_evidence_context: Table 1: Summary of previous findings that the current research attempts to replicate.

targets.title: The future looks “right”: effects of the horizontal location. of advertising images on product attitude
targets.evidence_quote: Chae and Hoegg ( 2013 ) Journal of Consumer Research 200 citations Study 2 n = 194 English-speaking participants from a national subject pool completed an online study -When participants are primed to desire a modern product, they were more favorable when it appeared on the right side of the advertisement - In contrast, when participants are primed to desire an antique, they are more favorable when the product appeared on the left Product attitude; F (2, 173) = 6.62, r = 0.189
targets.outcome_quote: No studies involving visual factors, between-participant manipulation of senses, or interactions between factors could be replicated.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The visual-factor set verdict covers this target. The results describe neither of the hypothesized simple effects as present. The text labels p=.064 significant, but the explicit overall failure verdict governs.
targets.target_evidence_context: Table 1: Summary of previous findings that the current research attempts to replicate.

targets.authors: Cian, L., Krishna, A., Elder, R. S.
targets.title: This logo moves me: dynamic imagery from static images
targets.evidence_quote: Cian et al. ( 2014 ) Journal of Marketing Research 229 citations Study 1 n = 74 Undergraduate students from a large university in the western US - A logo that evokes greater perceived movement (logo dynamism) generates more favorable attitudes toward the brand Attitudes toward the brand; F (1, 72) = 5.26, r = 0.261
targets.outcome_quote: No studies involving visual factors, between-participant manipulation of senses, or interactions between factors could be replicated.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The visual-factor set verdict covers this target. The manipulation affected perceived movement, but the central brand-attitude effect was absent.
targets.target_evidence_context: Table 1: Summary of previous findings that the current research attempts to replicate.

targets.authors: Madzharov, a V., Block, L. G.
targets.title: Effects of product unit image on consumption of snack foods
targets.evidence_quote: Madzharov and Block ( 2010 ) Journal of Consumer Psychology 161 citations Study 1A n = 37 Undergraduate business students from a large Northeastern university - Packages with more product units displayed on the package are perceived to contain more product quantity than packages with fewer product units displayed on the package Product quantity; F (1, 35) = 6.93, r = 0.407 Serving size; F (1, 35) = 4.83, r = 0.348
targets.outcome_quote: No studies involving visual factors, between-participant manipulation of senses, or interactions between factors could be replicated.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The visual-factor set verdict covers this target. Neither product quantity nor serving size showed the original effect.

reasoning: Verified title, authors Kosuke Motoki and Sayo Iseki, DOI, article boundaries, full results and reference list. This completed project collected fresh Japanese online data to retest ten published papers. Targets are the ten papers actually included in Table 1 and Results. The introduction mentions Lowrey and Shrum (2007), but it is not an additional tested target: Table 1 and Results identify Shrum et al. (2012) as the actual target. One entry per original paper; the replication sections are named by author rather than assigned study numbers. All citation data and DOIs are transcribed from the supplied reference list, retaining its apparent punctuation and initial errors. Overall authors' target-specific verdicts take precedence over individual tests. No FORRT sources or other coder outputs were consulted.
